5190.label: S/T-rich low-complexity IDRs
5190.summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat tracts—especially Ser/Thr‑ and Pro‑rich segments—forming long flexible tails or linkers (often C‑terminal); includes mucin‑like S/T‑rich extracellular regions and polar LCRs in diverse proteins.
5190.description:
Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat tracts—especially Ser/Thr‑ and Pro‑rich segments—forming long flexible tails or linkers (often C‑terminal); includes mucin‑like S/T‑rich extracellular regions and polar LCRs in diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Long regional activation spanning tens to hundreds of residues within low‑pLDDT, coil-rich IDRs; punctuated peaks along tandem repeats; minimal/absent in folded domains; frequently enriched toward C‑terminal regions and often commencing after signal peptides in secreted proteins.
Exemplars: - Semenogelins (gel-forming seminal plasma proteins): strong activation across the tandem repeat–rich, disordered mature chain; inactive on the N‑terminal signal peptide.
- FHA-domain proteins with long disordered tails: activation confined to the low‑complexity C‑terminal IDR; no activation in the structured FHA domain.
- DNA ligases: activation on disordered linkers and low‑confidence coil segments, including C‑terminal flexible regions.
- Shigella invasion effector IpaA: activation on polar, compositionally biased disordered C‑terminal region and other low‑pLDDT patches.

6717.label: Principal folded core domain
6717.summary: A structural signal for the principal folded core domain—most often the mid-to-C-terminal catalytic or structural lobe—characterized by long, basic/hydrophobic, well-structured segments; it highlights the main substrate/ligand‑interacting or assembly domain while sparing N‑terminal disordered or accessory modules.
6717.description:
Summary: A structural signal for the principal folded core domain—most often the mid-to-C-terminal catalytic or structural lobe—characterized by long, basic/hydrophobic, well-structured segments; it highlights the main substrate/ligand‑interacting or assembly domain while sparing N‑terminal disordered or accessory modules.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long contiguous activation blocks with multiple peaks within alpha-helices and beta-strands; typically strongest in mid-to-C-terminal regions of long proteins; often includes residues forming basic patches or metal/ligand contacts but is not confined to catalytic residues; minimal activation in N-terminal IDRs or accessory domains (e.g., PLAT, PX, PAZ).
Exemplars: - 5′–3′ exoribonuclease (XRN family): activation across the large catalytic core in the N-terminal half.
- Plant lipoxygenase: strong activation over the C-terminal dioxygenase catalytic domain, including Fe-coordinating histidines.
- Argonaute proteins: concentrated activation on the C-terminal Piwi RNase H–like domain, not on the PAZ domain.
- Tyrosyl‑DNA phosphodiesterase (PLD superfamily): activation across the C-terminal catalytic domain, emphasizing DNA‑interaction surface rather than the HxK catalytic histidines.
- cGAS-like nucleotidyltransferase: broad activation over the C-terminal lobe/regulatory surface distinct from the N-terminal Mg2+-binding site.
- Viral major capsid proteins: activation on the C-terminal structural region implicated in assembly/genome engagement.
- Sorting nexin (PX–BAR family): activation on the C-terminal helical BAR-like region downstream of the PX domain.

6727.label: Non-catalytic structural scaffold
6727.summary: Broad, non-catalytic structural context within and around functional domains—covering peripheral helices, strands, and loop segments—while de-emphasizing the precise catalytic and metal-ligating residues
6727.description:
Summary: Broad, non-catalytic structural context within and around functional domains—covering peripheral helices, strands, and loop segments—while de-emphasizing the precise catalytic and metal-ligating residues
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation over tens to hundreds of residues, spanning mixed coil/helix/strand segments within catalytic cores and adjacent subdomain scaffolds; catalytic ligands (e.g., metal-binding His/Cys, catalytic Tyr/Asp) are typically de-emphasized, with occasional sharp single-residue peaks—sometimes glycine—at loop/helix caps or flexible turns; activation can extend into well-ordered helices and strands

6756.label: Phosphate/acyl transfer catalytic cores
6756.summary: Domain-level cores of phosphate- or acyl-group–handling catalytic modules: acidic, helical, hydrophobic-rich segments that house either catalytic Asp/Glu for Mg2+-dependent phosphodiester/nucleotidyl transfer (or metal coordination) or Ser-His-Asp catalytic triads of alpha/beta-hydrolase lipase-like folds; seen across HECT E3 catalytic lobes, DDE/derived transposase DNA-binding/catalytic regions (THAP/BED/FAR1-FHY3), NTase enzymes (cGAS/cGLR), primases/polymerase-related proteins, ribonucleotide reductase R1 cores, the helical subdomain of PX phosphoinositide-binding domains, and lipase-like EDS1/PAD4 family proteins.
6756.description:
Summary: Domain-level cores of phosphate- or acyl-group–handling catalytic modules: acidic, helical, hydrophobic-rich segments that house either catalytic Asp/Glu for Mg2+-dependent phosphodiester/nucleotidyl transfer (or metal coordination) or Ser-His-Asp catalytic triads of alpha/beta-hydrolase lipase-like folds; seen across HECT E3 catalytic lobes, DDE/derived transposase DNA-binding/catalytic regions (THAP/BED/FAR1-FHY3), NTase enzymes (cGAS/cGLR), primases/polymerase-related proteins, ribonucleotide reductase R1 cores, the helical subdomain of PX phosphoinositide-binding domains, and lipase-like EDS1/PAD4 family proteins.

Activation pattern: Long, contiguous domain-level activation over folded cores; strongest within helical subdomains or alpha/beta-hydrolase cores around conserved catalytic residues (Asp/Glu or Ser-His-Asp triad); aligns with C-terminal catalytic regions in HECT E3s and the C-terminal half of PX domains; tracks structured cores rather than short motifs.

Exemplars:
- HECT-type E3 ubiquitin ligases: activation on the C-terminal HECT catalytic lobe.
- Transposases and transposon-derived DNA-binding proteins (DDE transposases, THAP, BED, PiggyBac; FAR1/FHY3 TFs): activation over acidic DDE cores or Zn-finger segments.
- CD-NTase enzymes (cGAS/cGLR): activation across the NTase catalytic core.
- DNA primases/polymerase-related enzymes: activation on DxD/DExD metal-binding segments and surrounding catalytic core.
- Ribonucleotide reductase R1 subunits: activation within the catalytic/interaction core.
- Sorting nexins/VPS family: activation in the PX domain’s C-terminal helical subdomain.
- Lipase-like alpha/beta-hydrolase immune regulators (EDS1/PAD4 family): activation over the N-terminal ABH core near the Ser-Asp-His catalytic triad (often partially degenerate).

8571.label: Generic electrostatic interface patches
8571.summary: Surface-exposed polar/charged interaction patches—typically flexible loops and helix–coil boundaries that flank catalytic or cofactor-binding motifs—representing a generic electrostatic interface signal rather than a specific catalytic motif.
8571.description:
Summary: Surface-exposed polar/charged interaction patches—typically flexible loops and helix–coil boundaries that flank catalytic or cofactor-binding motifs—representing a generic electrostatic interface signal rather than a specific catalytic motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks dispersed across the sequence; enriched in low-to-medium confidence/disordered segments and at helix–coil transitions, with additional signal on exposed helical faces; often adjacent to (but not centered on) catalytic residues or ligand/cofactor-binding sites; coverage ranges from sparse peaks to diffuse stretches across large proteins.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-Cas13a endoribonuclease (HEPN nuclease): peaks on polar residues across flexible regions within and outside HEPN domains, avoiding the core catalytic residues yet flanking functional areas.
- Bacterial ElaD-like cysteine protease/deubiquitinase: peaks on Gly/Ser/Thr-rich coils and nearby helices away from the Cys/His catalytic dyad, consistent with surface loops used for interactions.
- ERO1-like FAD-dependent thiol oxidase: peaks at helix–coil transitions adjacent to the redox-active Cys motif and near the FAD-binding region, with little signal on the N-terminal signal peptide.

8832.label: Acidic low-complexity linkers
8832.summary: Low-complexity coil/linker-like segments enriched for acidic/polar and small residues (S/T/D/E/N/G with frequent P), often near domain boundaries and in terminal tails, and also appearing on loop-like residues bordering structured catalytic regions; these positions are frequently phosphorylation- or interaction-prone connectors.
8832.description:
Summary: Low-complexity coil/linker-like segments enriched for acidic/polar and small residues (S/T/D/E/N/G with frequent P), often near domain boundaries and in terminal tails, and also appearing on loop-like residues bordering structured catalytic regions; these positions are frequently phosphorylation- or interaction-prone connectors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on isolated residues or very short microsegments, scattered across the sequence; commonly on S/T/D/N/G/P residues in coil contexts, interdomain linkers, acidic stretches, and disordered tails, with occasional peaks at the start of α-helices or at boundaries between domains.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid (N) protein: peaks at the CTD boundary and in the C-terminal disordered tail on S/T sites annotated as phosphorylated.
- CRISPR Cas13a endoribonuclease: multiple peaks in low-confidence coil loops, especially the flexible linker between the two HEPN domains and other interdomain/terminal linkers.
- Adenylate cyclase/hemolysin toxin (CyaA-type): activation within an Ala/Gly-rich low-complexity hemolysin region required for partner interaction, and on loop/linker residues adjacent to catalytic segments.
- Herpesvirus DNA replication helicase: sparse peaks on S/T/D residues in loop-like contexts within the helicase chain, outside ATP-binding motifs.

10197.label: Charged catalytic channel segments
10197.summary: Charged and mixed-composition segments that form or flank catalytic channels of large polymer- and nucleotide-handling machines, particularly the active-site cores of DDE-type recombinases/transposases and the channel-lining regions of bacteriophage portal proteins; the same physico-chemical signature can also appear in cytosolic channel loops of TMEM16/anoctamins and in acidic catalytic channels of some carbohydrate-active hydrolases.
10197.description:
Summary: Charged and mixed-composition segments that form or flank catalytic channels of large polymer- and nucleotide-handling machines, particularly the active-site cores of DDE-type recombinases/transposases and the channel-lining regions of bacteriophage portal proteins; the same physico-chemical signature can also appear in cytosolic channel loops of TMEM16/anoctamins and in acidic catalytic channels of some carbohydrate-active hydrolases.

Activation pattern: Primarily long, contiguous regional activation (tens to hundreds of residues) in the mid-to-C-terminal portions of very large proteins, often spanning a structured helix or strand into adjacent coil segments around the catalytic/pore lining; frequent enrichment for acidic/basic residues with scattered glycines. Secondary mode: sharp residue-level peaks at individual catalytic carboxylates within these regions. In membrane channels, activation can extend from a cytosolic regulatory loop into an adjacent transmembrane helix.

Exemplars:
- V(D)J recombination-activating protein 1 (RAG1) and related DDE-type recombination proteins: activation across the catalytic helix and surrounding charged, flexible segments that bind DNA and metals, including the catalytic Asp/Glu and divalent-cation binding sites.
- Bacteriophage portal proteins: activation on channel-lining β-strand and adjacent regions that form the DNA translocation channel.
- Influenza-type viral polymerase acidic subunits: activation on extended C-terminal core-proximal segments adjacent to catalytic regions.
- Ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase large subunits: activation on long active-site/effector-channel–adjacent loops enriched in acidic/basic residues.
- AAA+ MCM helicase family: activation around ATP/Mg2+-coordinating and DNA-channel–adjacent charged loops (Walker-B–proximal region).
- mRNA capping/cap-modifying enzymes: activation across cap-binding/modification modules (triphosphatase, guanylyltransferase, and SAM-dependent methyltransferase regions).
- TMEM16/anoctamin channels: activation on a cytosolic Ca2+-responsive loop and into the adjoining transmembrane helix lining the conduction pathway.
- Nonribosomal peptide synthetase adenylation domains: occasional residue-level peak on a catalytic glutamate within an active-site helix coordinating Mg2+/ATP chemistry.
- Dynamin-like/P-loop NTPase GTPases: activation around P-loop/Switch I–II charged loops that coordinate Mg2+-NTP in the catalytic pocket.
- Carbohydrate-active glycoside hydrolases (e.g., beta-xylosidase): activation on acidic, channel-lining loops surrounding the catalytic acid/base residues.

10911.label: Glycine-anchored H/R micro-loops
10911.summary: A sequence-level detector for short glycine-anchored, His/Arg–bearing signature motifs that mark catalytic or binding micro-loops, most often at β→α junctions or helix N-caps. It highlights conserved kernels such as G/G–H/R flanked by small hydrophobics or acidic residues that define active/interaction sites across enzyme and scaffold families (e.g., Fic HPF–x–[D/E]–GNG–R; sulfiredoxin GG–CHR; primase IV/VEG; MutL IVVDQH), when these motifs are present and exposed.
10911.description:
Summary: A sequence-level detector for short glycine-anchored, His/Arg–bearing signature motifs that mark catalytic or binding micro-loops, most often at β→α junctions or helix N-caps. It highlights conserved kernels such as G/G–H/R flanked by small hydrophobics or acidic residues that define active/interaction sites across enzyme and scaffold families (e.g., Fic HPF–x–[D/E]–GNG–R; sulfiredoxin GG–CHR; primase IV/VEG; MutL IVVDQH), when these motifs are present and exposed.

Activation pattern: Short, contiguous windows (5–15 residues) with sharp residue-level peaks centered on conserved glycine-rich motifs with nearby His/Arg; minimal signal outside these motifs. Frequently maps to a β-strand followed by the start of an α-helix or N-terminal helix-capping segments; also captures gly–gly–rich tails in some nucleases. Protein-level activation may be modest if the motif is very short or masked.

Exemplars:
- Fic/Doc AMPylases and Fic-like effectors: activation on the canonical HPF–x–[D/E]–G–N–G–R catalytic signature (strong/consistent; e.g., FICD shows moderate signal).
- Sulfiredoxins: strong peaks on the GG–C–H–R active-site loop (consistent).
- BTB/POZ and Kelch-domain proteins: observed only in subsets with basic/GG–H/R N-cap segments; many eukaryotic Kelch proteins (e.g., gigaxonin) are weak/absent.
- Chromosome partitioning/nucleoid regulators (e.g., KorB/Noc): β→α junctions centered on H–G followed by an Arg-rich helix (often strong).
- DnaG primases and RNase M5: subset with an exposed I/V–I/V–E–G loop; many homologs (e.g., some mycoplasma primases) are weak/absent.
- tRNA isopentenyltransferases/dimethylallyltransferases: recurrent R…[I/V][I/V]G motif in the active-site loop when present.
- Excinuclease UvrC: only some homologs with C-terminal gly–gly–rich tails activate; many are silent.
- Mismatch-repair endonucleases (MutL/PMS2/MLH3): primarily bacterial MutL-like proteins with accessible IVVDQH; eukaryotic PMS2/MLH3 often weak/absent.
- Viral proteins: select small effectors with glycine-rich H/R patches; large polymerase subunits (e.g., influenza PB2) generally do not activate.

11980.label: Small-residue membrane helix hotspots
11980.summary: Small-residue hotspots (primarily Gly/Ser/Ala, occasionally Pro) in alpha-helical segments that engage membranes—within transmembrane helices and their flanking caps, and in membrane-interacting amphipathic helices—across transporters, membrane enzymes, and membrane-associated trafficking proteins.
11980.description:
Summary: Small-residue hotspots (primarily Gly/Ser/Ala, occasionally Pro) in alpha-helical segments that engage membranes—within transmembrane helices and their flanking caps, and in membrane-interacting amphipathic helices—across transporters, membrane enzymes, and membrane-associated trafficking proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in TM helices and at helical boundaries, and in amphipathic membrane-binding helices; enriched for small residues; repeated across multi-pass proteins but also present in single-pass and peripheral membrane proteins; little to no signal in beta strands or unstructured tails; peaks mark specific sites rather than whole helices.
Exemplars:
- Claudins and TARP/claudin-like gamma subunits: hotspots within TM helices and at entry/exit; loops/glycosylation sites inactive.
- MFS transporters and FtsK N-termini: discrete peaks in each membrane helix; cytosolic ATPase or soluble domains inactive.
- Multispan glycosyltransferases (e.g., GPI mannosyltransferases): selective hotspots in TM helices; luminal/proline-rich tails inactive.
- Lipoprotein signal peptidase II: peaks across multiple TMs.
- Apolipoprotein L family: hotspots in the C-terminal membrane-anchoring helix.
- Sorting nexins/retromer adaptors: peaks in amphipathic, membrane-binding helices despite lacking transmembrane segments.

15048.label: Domain boundary amphipathic helices
15048.summary: Amphipathic alpha-helical/coiled-coil segments positioned at domain termini (often C-terminal) that serve as oligomerization/linker or anchoring helices; this includes terminal transmembrane helices with charged juxtamembrane flanks and short terminal helices that buttress catalytic cores in integrase/nuclease-derived modules.
15048.description:
Summary: Amphipathic alpha-helical/coiled-coil segments positioned at domain termini (often C-terminal) that serve as oligomerization/linker or anchoring helices; this includes terminal transmembrane helices with charged juxtamembrane flanks and short terminal helices that buttress catalytic cores in integrase/nuclease-derived modules.
Activation pattern: Regional activation: long, continuous tracts over helices (coiled-coils or a final TM helix plus its flanks), with residue-level peaks centered in helical cores; strong bias to C-terminal regions and domain boundaries; may encompass catalytic residues when these reside on a helix; typically avoids canonical zinc-finger motifs and most other TM helices; not driven by generic disorder.
Exemplars: - Retroelements/integrase fusions (NYNRIN): short C-terminal helix within the integrase catalytic core is specifically highlighted.
- SPX–EXS family transporters (SYG1/EXS): the final EXS transmembrane helix and its immediate extra- and cytosolic juxtamembrane segments are selected, while other TMs are not.
- FAR1/FRS transcription factors (Mutator-like transposase-derived): central coiled-coil linker between the MULE transposase-derived domain and the SWIM zinc finger shows sustained activation.
- BED zinc-finger nuclear proteins (VID22-like): extended C-terminal helical tracts (coiled-coil-like) are strongly activated, whereas the BED finger and unrelated single TM segment are not.

8070.label: N-terminal secretion/docking SLiMs
8070.summary: Short linear N‑terminal targeting/docking motifs in low‑complexity regions—most often immediately downstream of a signal peptide in small secreted peptides/effectors and, by analogy, proline‑rich interaction motifs in cytosolic adaptor proteins—that mediate secretion/host translocation or partner recruitment (e.g., RxLR-type host‑targeting tracts in oomycete effectors and EVH1‑binding proline‑rich segments in LIM‑domain adaptors)
8070.description:
Summary: Short linear N‑terminal targeting/docking motifs in low‑complexity regions—most often immediately downstream of a signal peptide in small secreted peptides/effectors and, by analogy, proline‑rich interaction motifs in cytosolic adaptor proteins—that mediate secretion/host translocation or partner recruitment (e.g., RxLR-type host‑targeting tracts in oomycete effectors and EVH1‑binding proline‑rich segments in LIM‑domain adaptors)
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks concentrated at a single site per protein; frequently near the N‑terminus (especially just after signal peptides in precursors), but also at internal short, non‑disordered tracts within otherwise disordered/low‑complexity regions; the marked residue within the SLiM is variable (no strong single‑amino‑acid preference). In zyxin‑like proteins the feature spikes in the N‑terminal half at a short ordered stretch amid proline‑rich low‑complexity regions, with additional isolated peaks on nearby prolines.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation in the short N‑terminal region proximal to the RxLR/EER host‑translocation segment immediately following the signal peptide (often just upstream or partially overlapping that tract).
- Plant small secreted signaling peptide precursors (CLE/CEP/IDA/PROPEP): activation just downstream of the signal peptide within the short leader/processing region that routes the propeptide for secretion.
- Vertebrate neuroendocrine hormone/neuropeptide precursors: a single N‑terminal peak near the signal peptide/pro‑region that governs secretory trafficking and processing.
- Animal toxins and antimicrobial peptides (especially proline‑rich AMPs/toxin propeptides): activation on a short secretion/docking motif in the N‑terminal low‑complexity segment of the precursor.
- Viral accessory/small structural host‑interaction proteins: activation on a short host‑mimicking docking SLiM in an N‑terminal low‑complexity region used for host engagement.
- LIM‑domain cytoskeletal adaptors (zyxin/LPP/TRIP6): activation within the N‑terminal proline‑rich EVH1‑binding region that recruits Ena/VASP.
- Mammalian reproductive/testis‑associated microproteins and p53/apoptosis‑related microproteins: activation on short linear interaction motifs embedded in intrinsically disordered regions.

3398.label: Ser/Pro-rich disordered tails
3398.summary: Serine/proline–rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered segments, especially terminal tails, linkers, and N‑terminal signal-peptide regions of small or secreted proteins; structured catalytic cores are largely ignored.
3398.description:
Summary: Serine/proline–rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered segments, especially terminal tails, linkers, and N‑terminal signal-peptide regions of small or secreted proteins; structured catalytic cores are largely ignored.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over disordered, low-pLDDT tracts (often at N- or C-termini) and along repetitive Ser/Pro-rich sequences; sparse residue-level peaks appear in flexible loops within otherwise ordered domains; can extend across signal peptides in precursors.
Exemplars: - Human regulatory protein ST20: weak, sparse peaks in an N‑terminal low-confidence helix within a largely disordered protein.
- Lipoyl synthase (Radical SAM enzyme): strong activation on disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; central Radical SAM core remains inactive.
- Conotoxin precursor (secreted peptide toxin): activation across the N‑terminal signal peptide helix and additional low-confidence regions of the mature toxin.
- WTUN1-like small eukaryotic protein: peaks at Ser/Pro residues within an annotated disordered C‑terminal region and additional low-confidence N‑terminal segments.
- Bacterial DNA ligase: activation in an annotated disordered insertion and flexible, low-confidence loops inside the ligase domain.

6484.label: Prion-like low-complexity IDRs
6484.summary: Polar low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—especially Q/N-rich (prion-like) segments and S/T- and glycine-rich tracts with simple SG/TG/PG repeats—typically located in inter-domain linkers and terminal tails of eukaryotic proteins and often harboring Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites.
6484.description:
Summary: Polar low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—especially Q/N-rich (prion-like) segments and S/T- and glycine-rich tracts with simple SG/TG/PG repeats—typically located in inter-domain linkers and terminal tails of eukaryotic proteins and often harboring Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites.
Activation pattern: Strong, contiguous regional activation restricted to predicted-disordered, low-complexity stretches (low pLDDT), with little to no signal in folded domains; superimposed residue-level peaks in dense S/T clusters, poly-Q/N or poly-G runs, and short unstructured linkers embedded within otherwise structured regions.
Exemplars: - Putative lipase ROG1 — activation on the C-terminal disordered acidic/polar tail; no signal in the structured catalytic region.
- Cyclic GMP-binding protein D (Ras-GEF/GRAM-containing signaling scaffold) — activation across long low-complexity disordered linkers between domains and a Q/N/S/G-rich C-terminal tail; inactive on Ras-GEF and GRAM domains.
- TRAPP complex subunit 10 — activation on an N-terminal LCD and multiple Q/N/G/S-rich disordered segments, including poly-G and terminal poly-Asn tracts, plus a Q-rich helical patch.
- SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling subunit SWI1 — strong activation over the N-terminal prion-like domain; additional spikes at short unstructured linkers in the C-terminus; no activation in the folded ARID domain.
- Post-transcriptional regulator Mkt1 — activation on short disordered S/T-rich segments that include known phosphoserine sites; structured regions remain largely inactive.

3585.label: Beta-strand boundary motif
3585.summary: Generic structural motif recognizing short loop/turn segments at the entrances and edges of beta-strands (beta-strand N-caps, strand-edge residues, and loop→beta transitions), often enriched in small/polar/acidic residues (G, S, T, D, E) within well-ordered domains across diverse proteins
3585.description:
Summary: Generic structural motif recognizing short loop/turn segments at the entrances and edges of beta-strands (beta-strand N-caps, strand-edge residues, and loop→beta transitions), often enriched in small/polar/acidic residues (G, S, T, D, E) within well-ordered domains across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on many short, discrete segments scattered through structured domains; strongest at coil-to-beta transitions and the first few residues of beta-strands, with occasional signal within short beta-strands or adjacent helices; minimal activity in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or highly disordered/low-confidence regions; can coincide with functional sites that reside on these structural boundaries (e.g., ligand-binding strands) but is not function-specific
Exemplars: - Glycoside hydrolases (alpha-L-fucosidase): multiple peaks on loops immediately preceding beta-strands and within short beta segments in the catalytic domain; signal peptide inactive
- HECT-type E3 ubiquitin ligases (UPL7): clustered peaks in the C-terminal HECT domain on coils/strand boundaries, including near the catalytic cysteine
- RING-type E3 ligases (DTX3): several loop→beta transitions and a short beta-strand outside the RING finger
- Mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (C3 toxin): strong peaks on NAD(+)-binding strand–loop–strand elements (beta-strands and adjacent loops) within the catalytic domain; signal peptide inactive
- Chromatin/DNA-binding SAND domain proteins (Sp100): dominant peak on a loop preceding a beta-strand within the SAND domain, plus a minor helical segment
- Thioester-containing complement-like glycoproteins (CD109/alpha-2-macroglobulin family): peaks on flexible loops and beta-strand edges in the extracellular domain; not at glycosylation or thioester sites
- Zona pellucida (ZP) extracellular matrix proteins (ZP1): focal activation at coil→beta transitions within the ZP domain; absent in signal peptide, transmembrane helix, and cytosolic tail
- Plant nuclear regulators (ASI1-interacting): activity confined to the structured C-terminal region (helices/beta), with little signal in the disordered N-terminus

6996.label: Disordered regions and linkers
6996.summary: Generic detection of intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity segments and helix–coil linkers/edges, especially in acidic/Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich regions, marking flexible tails and linkers rather than catalytic cores
6996.description:
Summary: Generic detection of intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity segments and helix–coil linkers/edges, especially in acidic/Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich regions, marking flexible tails and linkers rather than catalytic cores
Activation pattern: Sparse, low‑magnitude residue‑level peaks scattered across sequences; enriched in predicted disorder (low pLDDT) and at starts/ends of helices or coil linkers; variable coverage from single sites to many peaks; only occasional weak signals inside well‑ordered helices; rarely aligns with catalytic motifs
Exemplars: - Centrosomal scaffold/adaptor (Flattop): isolated peaks in N‑terminal coil and within an annotated disordered C‑terminal region.
- PP2A regulatory subunit (TAP46): strongest signal in a compositionally biased, disordered C‑terminal segment, with additional scattered peaks including one in a stable helix.
- Protein lysine methyltransferase (eEF1A‑KMT4): peak in an N‑terminal low‑confidence helix; minor peaks near, but not on, catalytic/consensus motifs, consistent with flexible termini or helix edges.
- Toxin–antitoxin antitoxin (MazE family): peaks at the linker between alpha helices and within moderate‑confidence helical segments.
- Bacterial transcriptional repressor (NRR homolog): highest peak at the start of a long helix immediately following a disordered N‑terminus (order–disorder transition).
- Actin capping protein inhibitor (CARMIL‑like): multiple peaks confined to annotated disordered, low‑pLDDT regions; little overlap with the structured interaction module.

9178.label: Phospho-regulated IDR scaffolds
9178.summary: Primarily eukaryotic (animals, fungi, and plants) intrinsically disordered, low-complexity scaffolding regions in very large components of multiprotein assemblies, enriched in polar/charged and Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly tracts (often phospho-regulated); the feature prefers IDRs and adjacent low-confidence helices/helix–coil transitions used for protein–protein interactions rather than stable folded domains. Also observed in large host-interacting viral scaffold/tegument proteins and, more rarely, large enzymatic regulators that contain extensive low-complexity regions.
9178.description:
Summary: Primarily eukaryotic (animals, fungi, and plants) intrinsically disordered, low-complexity scaffolding regions in very large components of multiprotein assemblies, enriched in polar/charged and Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly tracts (often phospho-regulated); the feature prefers IDRs and adjacent low-confidence helices/helix–coil transitions used for protein–protein interactions rather than stable folded domains. Also observed in large host-interacting viral scaffold/tegument proteins and, more rarely, large enzymatic regulators that contain extensive low-complexity regions.
Activation pattern: Domain-scale, sustained activation across long IDRs and mixed helix–coil segments with low structural confidence; relative suppression over continuous, high-pLDDT helical regions. Residue-level peaks on Ser/Thr clusters (frequent phosphosites), acidic/basic runs, and Pro/Gly-rich low-complexity motifs; occasional spikes in short coiled segments embedded within disorder. Activation commonly concentrates in N- to mid-sequence tracts and can reappear at termini, spanning hundreds of residues.
Exemplars: - Ribosome biogenesis/nucleolar assembly factors: strong signal on N-/mid-sequence low-confidence helices and helix–coil linkers; reduced on the well-structured C-terminal helical block.
- mRNA processing/splicing cofactor (Virilizer-like): very high activation across long disordered, charged low-complexity blocks and a short coiled segment; local peaks at Ser/Thr and Pro/Arg repeats.
- Cell-junction/polarity scaffold (Discs lost-like): high activation on disordered, polar Ser/Gly/Pro-rich stretches and adjacent low-confidence helices; includes annotated phosphoserines.
- Ion-channel complex scaffold (UNC79-like): extended activation on low-confidence helix–coil regions with Pro runs and Lys/Arg clusters; muted on long, confident helices.
- Mediator/Integrator complex subunits: strong activation across long IDRs and coiled regions used for transcriptional coactivator scaffolding; muted on more continuous high-confidence helices.
- Viral tegument scaffolds (e.g., HCMV UL32/pp150): broad activation on extensive low-complexity acidic/basic tracts.
- Rare large enzymatic regulators (e.g., TARBP1/TRP-185-like methyltransferases): activation concentrates in their extensive IDR/low-complexity segments flanking or inserted within catalytic architecture.

15329.label: Terminal intrinsically disordered regions
15329.summary: Intrinsic structural disorder: long, unannotated terminal extensions and other extended segments outside annotated catalytic/structured domains (typically coil, low pLDDT), with low activation in well-folded domain cores
15329.description:
Summary: Intrinsic structural disorder: long, unannotated terminal extensions and other extended segments outside annotated catalytic/structured domains (typically coil, low pLDDT), with low activation in well-folded domain cores
Activation pattern: Regional activation across contiguous intrinsically disordered stretches (often tens to hundreds of residues), frequently at N- or C-termini; sharp drop at boundaries entering folded, high-confidence domains; no specific residue-type preference
Exemplars: - Nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS megaenzyme): strong activation on the N-terminal pre-domain segment and a short C-terminal tail flanking the condensation/adenylation/carrier domains; low activation within the structured catalytic modules.
- Secreted bacterial protease (PrtH family): highest activation across a long, unannotated C-terminal extension predicted to be disordered; minimal activation in the structured N-terminal/catalytic regions.
- Aspartate–/Asparagine–tRNA ligase (aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase): strong activation over a long N‑terminal disordered region preceding the catalytic core, with activation dropping sharply in the folded enzyme domain and rising modestly again in a flexible C‑terminal tail.

10371.label: DNA/RNA-binding regulatory domains
10371.summary: Nucleic acid–interaction modules of nuclear/chromatin regulatory proteins and viral regulators—covering both structured DNA-binding domains (e.g., BEN domain, CHC2-type zinc fingers) and compositionally biased, charged Ser/Thr–rich disordered regions used as transcriptional activation or RNA-processing/export segments.
10371.description:
Summary: Nucleic acid–interaction modules of nuclear/chromatin regulatory proteins and viral regulators—covering both structured DNA-binding domains (e.g., BEN domain, CHC2-type zinc fingers) and compositionally biased, charged Ser/Thr–rich disordered regions used as transcriptional activation or RNA-processing/export segments.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional/domain-level activation across long contiguous segments enriched in S, T, E, D, K, and R; sustained signal over entire DNA/RNA-binding domains or regulatory IDRs. Peaks can coincide with DNA/RNA-contacting helices and Zn-coordinating Cys/His, but the feature does not mark generic disorder—rather, it selects regulatory nucleic-acid–engaging segments.
Exemplars: - Viral nuclear antigens (e.g., EBNA family): strong activation over central acidic/Ser/Thr–rich disordered transactivation regions, while other low-complexity tails are not highlighted.
- Herpesvirus ICP27-like mRNA export factors: activation across the C-terminal CHC2-type zinc finger, including the Zn-binding Cys/His residues, consistent with RNA-binding/regulatory function.
- BEN-domain chromatin regulators (e.g., BEND5): robust activation within the C-terminal half of the BEN DNA-binding domain that mediates chromatin/DNA engagement.
- Sequence-specific nuclear transcription factors (e.g., LIN-14): activation within the helical core of the annotated DNA-binding region.

4137.label: Global structure-agnostic activation
4137.summary: A broadly active feature that fires across nearly the entire length of many proteins, covering both folded structural elements (β-strands, α-helices) and unstructured regions, without strong selectivity for a specific sequence motif, fold, or functional class.
4137.description:
Summary: A broadly active feature that fires across nearly the entire length of many proteins, covering both folded structural elements (β-strands, α-helices) and unstructured regions, without strong selectivity for a specific sequence motif, fold, or functional class.
Activation pattern: Dense, near-uniform activation across most residues of a protein, with moderate local peaks scattered through the sequence; folded catalytic cores, secondary-structure elements, and loop regions all carry comparable activation, and well-annotated low-complexity/disordered tracts are not preferentially highlighted.
Exemplars:
- Herpesvirus Major DNA-binding protein: activation spans virtually the entire chain, including the zinc finger and central folded region.
- Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (e.g., Dioicin-2): nearly all residues active across the folded catalytic chain.
- Archaeal CRISPR Cmr7: activation throughout the protein, with highest values on β-strands and helices.
- Plant seed lectin (Trichosanthes anguina): activation distributed across the folded α/β chains.
- Bacterial PPi-PEPCK: broad activation across the large folded enzyme.
- Ebola matrix protein VP40: activation across nearly all residues, including the membrane-binding region and structured β-strands.
- Viral capsid proteins: activation concentrated in the structured body of the capsid rather than in disordered terminal extensions.

11395.label: Spire KIND/WH2 with charged LCRs
11395.summary: Conserved motifs within the KIND domain and flanking the WH2 actin-binding motifs of Spire family actin nucleators, together with low-complexity, intrinsically disordered regions enriched in charged/polar residues (E/D/S/T/K/R) in other proteins; occasionally shows weaker signal within or flanking helical segments (e.g., transmembrane or coiled-coil boundaries).
11395.description:
Summary: Conserved motifs within the KIND domain and flanking the WH2 actin-binding motifs of Spire family actin nucleators, together with low-complexity, intrinsically disordered regions enriched in charged/polar residues (E/D/S/T/K/R) in other proteins; occasionally shows weaker signal within or flanking helical segments (e.g., transmembrane or coiled-coil boundaries).
Activation pattern: In Spire proteins, sharp residue-level peaks at conserved positions in/around the KIND domain and WH2 motifs (e.g., LTPYE, RVKK, WARFWVQ, CRAL contexts), with secondary weaker activation in helical/coiled-coil segments. In disordered/LCR-rich proteins, regional activation across long charged/polar stretches with many positions non-zero; residue-level peaks often at Ser/Thr/Lys/Arg/Pro.
Exemplars: - Spire family actin nucleators: strongest activation on conserved residues within the KIND domain and at WH2-flanking motifs, with weaker signal in adjacent coiled-coil and disordered linker regions.
- Disordered scaffold proteins (e.g., C4orf54): regional activation across multiple annotated disordered regions enriched in basic/acidic and polar residues.
- Mitochondrial precursor proteins with disordered N-terminal segments: activation across the disordered N-terminal region adjacent to the transit peptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., HCV E2 HVR1 and E1 region): strong activation on the disordered, hypervariable luminal HVR1; additional moderate signal in the adjacent C-terminal transmembrane helix.
- Secreted peptide hormone precursors: activation on disordered propeptides and Lys/Arg-rich processing segments rather than the hydrophobic signal peptide.
- Centrosomal/ciliary coiled-coil scaffolds: charged low-complexity segments and disordered termini flanking coiled-coil repeats.
- Peroxisome biogenesis/membrane proteins: cytosolic/luminal disordered loops and low-complexity tails, with occasional signal near TM boundaries.
- RNA processing/translation regulators: polar/charged low-complexity domains (e.g., RGG/RG-rich, Ser/Thr-rich) and flexible linkers.
- Protein kinases and deubiquitinases: intrinsically disordered N/C-terminal tails and flexible low-complexity linkers between domains.

- Peroxisome biogenesis/membrane proteins: cytosolic/luminal disordered loops and low-complexity tails, with occasional signal near TM boundaries.
- RNA processing/translation regulators: polar/charged low-complexity domains (e.g., RGG/RG-rich, Ser/Thr-rich) and flexible linkers.
- Protein kinases and deubiquitinases: intrinsically disordered N/C-terminal tails and flexible low-complexity linkers between domains.

5232.label: Short amphipathic helices
5232.summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helical segments that mediate assembly, nucleic-acid/protein binding, or membrane association; common in intrinsically disordered regions or flexible linkers, but also present as coiled-coils or small helix-bundles within otherwise structured proteins; occasionally overlap or flank transmembrane helices. Enriched in mixed charged and hydrophobic residues.
5232.description:
Summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helical segments that mediate assembly, nucleic-acid/protein binding, or membrane association; common in intrinsically disordered regions or flexible linkers, but also present as coiled-coils or small helix-bundles within otherwise structured proteins; occasionally overlap or flank transmembrane helices. Enriched in mixed charged and hydrophobic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with multiple discrete residue-level peaks on short helices; frequently in low-confidence/disordered helices, but also in stable amphipathic helices (coiled-coils, helix-bundle repeats) and, in some cases, within/near transmembrane segments.
Exemplars:
- Herpesvirus capsid triplex proteins (VP19C/VP23): amphipathic coiled-coil/helical segments used in capsid assembly.
- Arenavirus/Mononegavirales nucleoproteins and phosphoproteins: basic, disordered helices for RNA binding/oligomerization.
- Influenza polymerase subunits (PA, PB2): flexible helical linkers/low-confidence helices between domains.
- Legionella DrrA/SidM: N‑terminal amphipathic membrane-targeting helix and flexible helical segments.
- Chlamydia Tarp: repetitive/coiled-coil and disordered helical regions.
- Staphylococcal Protein A: small helix-bundle Ig-binding domains and C‑terminal membrane/sortase region with amphipathic/TM helices.
- CRISPR-Cas proteins (Cas13a and Cascade/Csy3/Cas7 family): flexible/linker or surface amphipathic helices within ribonucleoprotein assemblies.
- Apicomplexan rhoptry/high MW proteins (e.g., CLAG/RhopH, ROP3): scattered low-confidence helices including marginal/true TM segments in secreted precursors.
- Adenovirus structural/core proteins: basic amphipathic helices implicated in DNA binding/assembly.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors and bacterial Type III/IV effectors: MoRF-like helices within IDRs for host engagement.

5477.label: Disordered SLiMs and helices
5477.summary: Intrinsic-disorder–associated interaction segments: short linear motifs and nascent helices (often amphipathic) embedded in low-complexity, flexible regions that mediate scaffold/adaptor binding across diverse proteins (including viral proteins)
5477.description:
Summary: Intrinsic-disorder–associated interaction segments: short linear motifs and nascent helices (often amphipathic) embedded in low-complexity, flexible regions that mediate scaffold/adaptor binding across diverse proteins (including viral proteins)
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long intrinsically disordered regions with many dispersed, low-intensity sites; punctate residue-level peaks within short segments embedded in disorder, frequently just outside annotated structured domains; coverage scales with protein length (broad in large scaffolds, short stretches in small proteins); often overlaps compositionally biased/low-complexity segments without strong residue-type specificity
Exemplars: - A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs): activation in disordered N-terminal interaction regions involved in partner binding (e.g., DPY30/MCM2 interaction segments) with additional signals across IDRs.
- Dynein-axonemal assembly factors: strong activation in disordered, polar-biased regions and at coil→helix transitions within short helices used for assembly interactions.
- Regulator of G-protein signaling (RGS12): a peak immediately N-terminal to the GoLoco domain at a coil-to-helix boundary, with minor signals in flexible helical segments and diffuse activation in low-confidence regions.
- Centrosomal/ciliary coiled-coil scaffolds: activation in flexible linkers and coiled-coil segments within long coiled-coil/low-complexity architectures.
- Apoptosis/Bcl-2 pathway proteins: activation on BH3-like short helices and adjacent disordered segments that mediate partner binding.
- Cullin scaffold proteins: signals on disordered linkers/terminal tails and adaptor-binding regions adjacent to helical repeats.
- DNA repair/replication factors (e.g., FAN1): activation in flexible, compositionally biased connectors between domains where interaction motifs reside.
- Secreted neuropeptide/hormone precursors: broad activation across unstructured propeptide regions enriched for short processing/interaction motifs.
- Viral proteins from diverse families: short IDRs harboring host-binding SLiMs and helix-forming segments that fold upon binding.

15543.label: Retained transmembrane signal anchors
15543.summary: Hydrophobic transmembrane signal anchors and adjacent membrane–proximal interface regions, especially in viral envelope/structural membrane proteins and other integral membrane proteins; the feature favors long, retained TM helices enriched in aromatics (Y/W/F) with nearby cysteines, rather than short, cleaved signal peptides.
15543.description:
Summary: Hydrophobic transmembrane signal anchors and adjacent membrane–proximal interface regions, especially in viral envelope/structural membrane proteins and other integral membrane proteins; the feature favors long, retained TM helices enriched in aromatics (Y/W/F) with nearby cysteines, rather than short, cleaved signal peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous segments (≈18–35 aa) corresponding to TM helices and flanking membrane‑proximal regions; short cleavable signal peptides alone usually do not elicit strong activation.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/fusion proteins with retained TM anchors (e.g., baculovirus GP64/F-class fusion, herpesvirus gH/gB): activation on the C‑terminal TM anchor and adjacent aromatic/cysteine‑rich membrane‑proximal segments; accessory subunits lacking a TM (e.g., herpesvirus gL) are weak/negative.
- Eukaryotic single‑pass receptors and receptor‑type kinases: activation on the lone transmembrane signal anchor; the N‑terminal cleavable signal peptide alone is weak.
- Multi‑pass bacterial/archaeal/eukaryotic inner‑membrane proteins and transporters: activation on one or more α‑helical TM segments.
- Secreted proteins without a retained membrane anchor (e.g., plant RIPs like gelonin): generally not activated.

10424.label: S/T-rich low-complexity IDRs
10424.summary: Low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered or weakly predicted helical/coil tracts enriched in serine/threonine and/or proline/glycine and charged residues; these occur in secreted mucin‑like PTS repeats and polar/acidic–basic linkers, in cytosolic scaffolds, and as flexible insertions or termini within large enzymes and organellar proteins; they frequently contain O-/N‑glycosylation motifs when luminal/secreted and phosphorylation sites when cytosolic, and tend to connect or decorate structured domains rather than forming them.
10424.description:
Summary: Low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered or weakly predicted helical/coil tracts enriched in serine/threonine and/or proline/glycine and charged residues; these occur in secreted mucin‑like PTS repeats and polar/acidic–basic linkers, in cytosolic scaffolds, and as flexible insertions or termini within large enzymes and organellar proteins; they frequently contain O-/N‑glycosylation motifs when luminal/secreted and phosphorylation sites when cytosolic, and tend to connect or decorate structured domains rather than forming them.

Activation pattern:
- Domain-level: Reduced in conserved, well‑folded catalytic cores; broadly elevated across annotated Disordered, Low‑complexity, and Polar/Basic–Acidic biased regions, long low‑pLDDT helices/coils, terminal tails, and flexible repeat boundaries; can also highlight low‑complexity insertions within enzymatic proteins.
- Regional context: Peaks in long low‑pLDDT helices/coils and at boundaries between repeats/domains; variable on coiled‑coils (high when low‑pLDDT/low‑complexity, lower when confidently ordered).
- Residue-level: Local maxima on clustered S/T (and nearby N in N‑X‑S/T sequons) and in P/G‑ and acidic/lysine‑rich runs; recurrent moderate spikes in short linker motifs (e.g., GEKP) and at the starts of C2H2 fingers; does not specifically track catalytic/metal‑binding residues.

Exemplars:
- Secreted mucin‑like glycoproteins: strong activation across S/T/N‑rich disordered segments and glycosylation sequons; low on signal peptides and ordered helices.
- Telomere/scaffold and BRCA‑like large nuclear proteins: elevated on long S/T/P‑ and charge‑rich IDRs; low on hydrophobic, ordered stretches.
- C2H2 zinc‑finger transcription factors: off in KRAB/finger cores; periodic spikes at finger starts and GEKP linkers; highest on low‑confidence inter‑finger bridges.
- LINE‑1 retrotransposon–associated proteins: strong in acidic/basic‑biased disordered blocks with phospho‑S/T; weak over well‑ordered helix bundles.
- FHA‑ and ELMO‑domain proteins: silent in compact domains; on in extended low‑pLDDT helices and disordered, polar/charged tracts.
- Large enzymes/organellar proteins (e.g., plastid RNA polymerase fragments, dinoflagellate luciferase): activation on low‑complexity acidic/polar insertions and termini; low on conserved catalytic/metal‑binding motifs.
- Plant NLR/immune receptors: signal on low‑complexity linkers and termini flanking NB‑ARC/LRR cores.

10655.label: Aromatic-rich alpha/beta core domains
10655.summary: Long, aromatic-rich α/β core domains typified by the soluble ABBA-type (PT‑barrel) aromatic/indole/xanthone prenyltransferase fold, and cross-reactive to other proteins that present similarly long, contiguous β‑strand-and-helix blocks; the feature emphasizes compact α/β cores and structured blocks while generally de-emphasizing disordered tails, and can also mark N‑ or C‑terminal α/β appendage domains when they present similar secondary‑structure runs
10655.description:
Summary: Long, aromatic-rich α/β core domains typified by the soluble ABBA-type (PT‑barrel) aromatic/indole/xanthone prenyltransferase fold, and cross-reactive to other proteins that present similarly long, contiguous β‑strand-and-helix blocks; the feature emphasizes compact α/β cores and structured blocks while generally de-emphasizing disordered tails, and can also mark N‑ or C‑terminal α/β appendage domains when they present similar secondary‑structure runs
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation in long continuous blocks that usually begin after a short N‑terminal segment (~30–90 residues) and extend for 100–300+ residues; strongest signal tracks runs of contiguous β‑strands with adjacent helices and is compositionally biased toward hydrophobic/aromatic residues (frequent W/Y, often WW/WY near the start), short glycine-rich and GP motifs, and clusters/pairs of histidines; disordered or low-complexity segments are generally de-emphasized, though short interaction-rich tracts can be included; activation can shift to a terminal β‑strand appendage when present
Exemplars: - Soluble aromatic/indole/xanthone prenyltransferases (DMATS and other ABBA/PT‑barrel enzymes) from filamentous Ascomycete fungi (Aspergillus, Penicillium, Sordariomycetes) with additional Actinobacterial and cyanobacterial representatives: activation spans the central PT‑barrel core that binds DMAPP and the aromatic substrate, matching the WW/WY- and His-enriched entrance/core.
- Bacterial MAPK phosphothreonine lyases (OspF/SpvC family): activation centers on the catalytic α/β core containing the Lys/His acid–base machinery.
- Beta-glucuronidase: signal confined to the C‑terminal β‑strand‑rich domain, not the upstream catalytic elements.
- Viral nucleoprotein: high activation over the structured N-terminal RNA-binding core, with low signal on the disordered C-terminal phosphoprotein-binding tail.
- Shieldin complex subunit SHLD3: strong N‑terminal signal over the MAD2L2‑interacting helix/strand patch (including the PKRSPP motif) and a short adjacent tract, with weak activation across the distal C‑terminus.
- PH‑domain protein: silent across the N‑terminal PH β‑sandwich, switching on within and after a low‑complexity linker to mark a long, aromatic‑rich downstream domain.

7093.label: PTM-prone Pro/Cys-rich repeats
7093.summary: Proline-rich and cysteine/proline-rich low-complexity repeat segments, including disordered Pro/Ser/Thr-rich stretches and C-C-X-P keratin-associated repeats, often acting as PTM-prone regions (e.g., O-glycosylation/hydroxyproline in secreted plant peptides) across diverse taxa

Summary: Proline-rich and cysteine/proline-rich low-complexity repeat segments, including disordered Pro/Ser/Thr-rich stretches and C-C-X-P keratin-associated repeats, often acting as PTM-prone regions (e.g., O-glycosylation/hydroxyproline in secreted plant peptides) across diverse taxa
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks clustered within disordered coil regions, short low-complexity repeats, and Pro-rich tandem motifs; sparse or patchy activation across long IDRs
Exemplars: - Hyp-rich systemin (HypSys) peptide precursors (plant peptide hormones): activation on disordered mature peptide segments rich in proline, centered on hydroxyproline and O-glycosylation sites.
- Keratin-associated proteins (KAP5 family, ultrahigh-sulfur): activation on cysteine residues within C-C-X-P tandem repeats.
- Serine/threonine protein kinases (eukaryotic): activation in long, low-complexity C-terminal tails and linkers; absent from the structured kinase and zinc-finger domains.
- Plant virus small/accessory proteins (e.g., potyvirus proteins): dispersed activation across largely disordered, low-confidence coil-rich sequences.
- Insect cuticle proteins: activation on Pro/Ala/Val-rich tandem repeats typical of structural cuticle regions.

4379.label: N-terminal targeting/interaction module
4379.summary: N-terminal sequence segments — both intrinsically disordered tails and the first folded element (α-helix or β-strands) — used as generic targeting/interaction modules for membranes, nucleic acids, secretion/chaperone engagement, or partner binding
4379.description:
Summary: N-terminal sequence segments — both intrinsically disordered tails and the first folded element (α-helix or β-strands) — used as generic targeting/interaction modules for membranes, nucleic acids, secretion/chaperone engagement, or partner binding
Activation pattern: Regional activation with a strong N‑terminal bias, often spanning the first ~20–40 residues including the first structured element (α-helix or β-strand cluster) when present, or disordered N-terminal stretches adjacent to folded domains; secondary peaks can occur at internal amphipathic helices; residue-level maxima land on a mix of hydrophobic (Leu/Ile/Val/Ala), aromatic (Phe/Tyr/Trp), and basic (Lys/Arg) positions
Exemplars: - Phage anti-defense DNA-mimic Ocr: activation on the first N‑terminal α-helix (residues ~5–25), while later helices are not highlighted.
- Poxvirus poxin phosphodiesterase toxin: strong activation on a disordered N‑terminal segment (residues ~1–26) and a moderate peak on an internal amphipathic helix containing catalytic residues.
- KCTD (BTB/POZ) family: activation on the low-complexity, disordered C‑terminal region following the BTB domain (partner/substrate-interaction segment).
- Retroviral Gag (e.g., foamy virus): activation on the N‑terminal matrix region containing a polybasic, amphipathic helix used for membrane/RNA engagement.
- HIV Vif: activation on the basic/hydrophobic N‑terminal segment that mediates partner binding.
- Type III/IV secretion effectors: activation on N‑terminal secretion/chaperone-binding regions that are disordered and amphipathic.
- Ribosome-inactivating proteins (plant/fungal toxins): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides/propeptides (basic N-region plus hydrophobic core) for secretion.
- Nucleic acid–binding/packaging proteins (viral and bacterial): activation on arginine/lysine-rich amphipathic segments that contact RNA/DNA.
- E. coli toxin–antitoxin and stress-modulator proteins: activation on basic, hydrophobic low-complexity tails/short helices used for binding and regulation.
- TIP41 family (PP2A/Tap42 interactors): activation on the N-terminal β-strand-rich segment of the folded core.
- Photosynthesis/carboxysome-associated small proteins: activation on short targeting/encapsulation peptides (amphipathic helices) used for microcompartment association.

1401.label: Broad extracellular domain activation
1401.summary: Regional activation within mature, processed extracellular/cell-surface proteins of bacteria and archaea, including S-layer and cell-surface glycoproteins, autotransporter/sortase-anchored proteases, and secreted enzymes.
1401.description: Summary: Regional activation within mature, processed extracellular/cell-surface proteins of bacteria and archaea, including S-layer and cell-surface glycoproteins, autotransporter/sortase-anchored proteases, and secreted enzymes. Activation pattern: Broad regional activation spread over hundreds of residues of large secreted/surface protein chains, with peaks falling on diverse local contexts (often containing mixed polar and hydrophobic residues) within both structured and less-structured parts of the extracellular passenger; many adjacent residues co-activate and multiple long segments can light up within very large surface proteins. Exemplars: - Bacterial cell-surface zinc metalloproteases (e.g., pneumococcal ZmpB/ZmpC): broad activation across the extracellular chain. - S-layer proteins (e.g., Bacillus anthracis EA1, Deinococcus Hpi, Haloarcula S-layer glycoprotein): activation distributed across the mature surface chain. - Cell-surface lipoprotein Spiralin of Spiroplasma. - Extracellular CAZymes and glycoside hydrolases (e.g., Bacillus glucanase, Geobacillus alpha-amylase) and large secreted sialidases: regional activation within the mature secreted chain. - Gram-negative autotransporter adhesins: activation on passenger-domain stalks. - Serine-rich repeat adhesins (SRRPs) of streptococci/staphylococci. - Fungal/yeast adhesins (Als, Flo families). - SRCR/scavenger receptor cysteine-rich family glycoproteins. - Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein GP210/Nup210: activation on its luminal region. - Viral envelope/spike/coat glycoproteins (e.g., filovirus GP mucin-like domain, coronavirus S): activation on external segments.

15526.label: Polar low-complexity disordered regions
15526.summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in polar/acidic and amide residues—especially Q/E/S/T/P/G—often including proline‑rich tracts and S/T clusters; these segments are flexible, cysteine‑poor, and typically lie outside structured catalytic cores (e.g., disordered tails, propeptides, and regulatory regions).

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in polar/acidic and amide residues—especially Q/E/S/T/P/G—often including proline‑rich tracts and S/T clusters; these segments are flexible, cysteine‑poor, and typically lie outside structured catalytic cores (e.g., disordered tails, propeptides, and regulatory regions).
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks concentrated within intrinsically disordered, low‑pLDDT segments; when long low‑complexity tracts are present, activation can extend across broad regions. Little to no activation in well‑folded domains.

10117.label: Diffuse low-complexity/disorder signature
10117.summary: A broadly tuned signature of disordered/low-complexity-containing proteins: the feature activates diffusely across long stretches of large multi-domain proteins, with residue-level peaks scattered through both folded and disordered segments. It is common in large, repeat-rich extracellular/surface proteins but also marks regions in diverse intracellular proteins.

- Large repeat-rich surface or ECM/cell-wall–like proteins from diverse taxa: activation spread across polar low-complexity segments interspersed with glycine/proline-containing turns.

6854.label: Low complexity helical repeats
6854.summary: A general, composition-driven signal for non-globular sequence regions: it prefers low-complexity, compositionally biased tracts and repetitive helical polymers, emphasizing charged/polar (E, D, K, R, S, Q) or Gly/Pro-rich content, and residues at helix–coil transitions; it is largely muted in compact, well-packed helical cores.

Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long low-complexity or repeat segments (coiled-coil stalks, collagenous repeats, disordered regulatory regions), with residue-level peaks at helix N/C caps and adjacent coils; minimal within stable helix cores; can span extensive stretches rather than a single short motif.

- Golgin/centrosomal/cytoskeletal coiled-coil scaffolds: sustained activation along long acidic/basic, low-complexity coiled-coil stalks.
- Extracellular-matrix collagens: activation across Gly–X–Y (often Gly–Pro–Hyp) repetitive triple-helix regions.
- Muscle long coiled-coil motors/partners (e.g., myosin/tropomyosin/titin segments): activation along extended coiled-coil helical repeats.
- Neuronal/presynaptic scaffolds: activation in coiled-coil/disordered linker regions that form extended scaffolds.
- Prokaryotic regulators (ECF sigma factors, toxin–antitoxin antitoxins, two-component histidine kinases): activation on acidic/basic low-complexity segments, helix–loop caps, and helical linkers/coiled-coils.

11769.label: Acidic IDR helical docking motifs
11769.summary: Protein-protein interaction elements—alpha-helical docking/oligomerization helices and short motifs within acidic, Ser/Pro/Gly-rich low-complexity segments—that mediate partner binding and scaffolding across diverse proteins and taxa.

- Kinases and other signaling enzymes: activation on regulatory/docking helices or accessory coiled-coil segments that mediate complex formation.
- Phosphatase regulators/partners (PP1/PP2A modulators): activation on helical docking and scaffold-binding motifs.
- Bacterial small regulators and toxin-antitoxin antitoxins: activation on helical dimerization and toxin-binding elements (HTH/RHH/coiled-coil).
- Multidomain extracellular/scaffold precursors: activation on N-terminal disordered acidic/Pro-rich segments used for partner docking.

3003.label: Ero1 FAD-binding NPER motif
3003.summary: A sequence- and family-specific feature that marks the conserved Ero1 oxidoreductase region surrounding the FAD-binding pocket, anchored by an invariant Asn in the VDLxxNPER[Y/F]T motif and accompanied by satellite peaks on conserved residues elsewhere in the Ero1 core.
3003.description:
Summary: A sequence- and family-specific feature that marks the conserved Ero1 oxidoreductase region surrounding the FAD-binding pocket, anchored by an invariant Asn in the VDLxxNPER[Y/F]T motif and accompanied by satellite peaks on conserved residues elsewhere in the Ero1 core.
Activation pattern: Strongest residue-level peak on the conserved Asn just upstream of the FAD-binding residues, with secondary peaks on a Lys in an upstream YKxxxx context and on additional conserved residues distributed across the Ero1 fold, including positions within annotated helices, strands, and turns of the structured core bracketed by the main disulfide bonds.
Exemplars: - Plant Ero1 (Arabidopsis ERO1, ERO2): dominant peak on Asn in the NPER motif near the FAD-binding site, with secondary peaks on a conserved Lys upstream and Gly/Ser residues in the structured core.
- Metazoan Ero1-like proteins (zebrafish ERO1-L-alpha, mouse ERO1-L-beta, Drosophila Ero1-like, C. elegans Ero1): same NPER-motif Asn peak plus conserved Lys and downstream Gly/Ser secondary peaks.
- Fungal Ero1 (S. cerevisiae, A. gossypii, K. lactis): same NPER-motif Asn peak with additional activations on residues within helices and strands of the Ero1 core.
- Herpesvirus tegument protein VP16: scattered peaks including isolated Gly residues and an Asn in a non-Ero1 context.

2363.label: Charged alpha-helical tracts
2363.summary: Polar/charged alpha-helical tracts (often low-complexity): E/D/K/R/S/T/N/Q-rich, low-aromatic segments occurring both in intrinsically disordered regions and as solvent-exposed helices within folded domains; these amphipathic/coiled-coil–like helices mediate oligomerization, nucleic-acid/protein binding, and assembly, especially in viral proteins.

Activation pattern: Regional—either long tracts in IDRs or multiple discrete peaks aligning to predicted alpha helices within charged segments of folded proteins; weak in hydrophobic/aromatic-dense cores.
Exemplars:
- Poxvirus morphogenesis/scaffold proteins: extended charged helical segments.
- Mononegavirus P and N/NP: charged coiled-coils and basic helix-prone RNA-binding tracts.
- Herpesvirus tegument/capsid/envelope (incl. gH/gL complexes): luminal charged helices for assembly.
- CRISPR Cas13a: polar/charged helical linkers and helix-rich surfaces flanking HEPN modules.
- Adenovirus DNA-binding/terminal/packaging proteins (incl. IIIa, terminal proteins): long charged helical segments.
- Bacterial type III secretion effectors: N-terminal charged, helix-prone secretion/chaperone-binding regions.
- Apicomplexan surface proteins: acidic/serine/asparagine repeat-rich helical stalks.
- Reoviridae/Bluetongue virus VP6 helicase: polar helices/linkers around the P-loop core.
- Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (e.g., pokeweed antiviral protein): solvent-exposed acidic/basic helical surfaces.

6943.label: Ordered helical segment marker
6943.summary: Residue-level signal for well-ordered alpha‑helical segments—covering coiled‑coils, soluble helices and, in some cases, transmembrane helices—rather than a specific sequence motif; the feature tends to mark stable helical cores and helix boundary/interface positions within structured regions while avoiding disordered tails.

Summary: Residue-level signal for well-ordered alpha‑helical segments—covering coiled‑coils, soluble helices and, in some cases, transmembrane helices—rather than a specific sequence motif; the feature tends to mark stable helical cores and helix boundary/interface positions within structured regions while avoiding disordered tails.
Activation pattern: Sparse, low‑amplitude residue‑level peaks scattered within one or more helical stretches of a structured region; often enriched at helix starts/ends or helix–membrane/interface zones; generally absent from disordered segments; occasionally spills into adjacent non‑helical residues within the same ordered domain.
Exemplars: - Cilia/flagella coiled‑coil protein (CFAP45): peaks confined to the structured, coiled‑coil C‑terminal half, highlighting residues inside helices and at a helix‑proximal coil; no signal in the disordered N‑terminus.
- Autophagy multi‑pass membrane protein (ATG9): scattered peaks in cytoplasmic helical segments and at a helix that transitions into the membrane; minor signal in a structured lumenal loop.
- ERAD mannosidase‑like lectin (EDEM1): sparse activation across the ordered lumenal catalytic domain; absent from the short cytosolic tail and the single transmembrane helix.
- Viral Vpu (HIV‑1): strong, localized activation within the single helical transmembrane segment; no activation in the disordered cytosolic tail.
- SPX‑domain vacuolar transporter component: activation concentrated at the start and within a long helix of the N‑terminal SPX domain; little/no signal in the downstream transmembrane region.

512.label: Short functional domain segments
512.summary: Short sequence segments distributed across diverse proteins, with peaks that often fall within structured catalytic, transporter, or fold-defining domains as well as occasional acidic/charged stretches and flexible linkers.

Activation pattern: Regional activation over short stretches (≈5–20 aa) with multiple noncontiguous activations per protein corresponding to separate segments.
Exemplars: - Enzymes with conserved catalytic folds (e.g., tryptophan biosynthesis IGPS, FolD, pectinesterase): activates within the catalytic region on short internal stretches
- Transporters (SWEET sugar transporters, ABC transporters): activates within transporter domains, often at cytoplasmic/extracellular loop junctions
- Protein kinases (e.g., CDK8): activates within the kinase domain on a short charged stretch
- Fungal regulatory/biosynthetic proteins (e.g., velvet complex subunit, nicotinate hydroxylase): activates within the core functional domain
- Organelle-targeted proteins: activates within the mature chain on acidic disordered stretches downstream of the cleaved targeting peptide
- Nucleic acid–binding/regulatory proteins (e.g., KIN17-like, RhoGEFs): activates on internal charged/zinc-finger-adjacent stretches

2519.label: Diffuse low-amplitude sequence-wide activation
2519.summary: Broadly distributed, low-amplitude feature that fires diffusely across many proteins, with frequent activation on polar residues (Thr, Ser) but also on charged and hydrophobic residues throughout both structured domains and disordered regions.
2519.description:
Summary: Broadly distributed, low-amplitude feature that fires diffusely across many proteins, with frequent activation on polar residues (Thr, Ser) but also on charged and hydrophobic residues throughout both structured domains and disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Many active positions per protein (often 10-15% of residues), with modest peak amplitudes; activations are scattered along the chain rather than concentrated at single sharp peaks, and span both folded domains and flanking disordered/low-complexity regions.
Exemplars:
- Viral structural proteins (capsids, membrane proteins, envelope glycoproteins): diffuse activation across the chain, including disordered N-terminal arms.
- Viral nucleoproteins and replication proteins (e.g., coronavirus N protein, herpesvirus DNA helicase, adenovirus DBP): activation distributed across both folded domains and disordered linkers/tails.
- Bacterial secreted enzymes (e.g., Streptomyces transglutaminases): activation across the propeptide and catalytic chain, including disordered regions enriched in basic/acidic residues.
- Eukaryotic regulatory proteins with mixed structured and disordered architecture.

- Cytoskeletal actin-related proteins (alpha-centractin) with C-terminal peaks

5765.label: Charged amphipathic helical surfaces
5765.summary: A broad, structural surface signal: solvent-exposed, ordered regions—most prominently alpha-helical segments—enriched in charged/polar residues (E, D, K, R, H, Q, S, T), marking amphipathic helical faces and other charged surface patches used for protein–protein assembly or domain packing.

Activation pattern: Regional activation across many sites in structured domains with residue-level peaks on charged/polar side chains, especially along alpha-helical faces; minimal signal in disordered termini/low-confidence regions; activation can extend over long stretches and across much of large multidomain proteins.
Exemplars: - RNA exosome nucleases (DIS3-like): activation on multiple C‑terminal alpha-helices with peaks at R/H/E; disordered N‑terminus inactive.
- Aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases: solvent-exposed helices in the catalytic core and anticodon-binding regions; charged helical faces and dimer/oligomer interfaces.
- DNA polymerases (cellular/archaeal/viral) and LigD: helical subdomains (thumb/fingers/auxiliary helices) and DNA/protein interface surfaces; peaks on K/R/E/D outside catalytic acidic motifs.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (GH31, GH3, alpha‑L‑fucosidase, 4‑alpha‑glucanotransferase): external helices around (alpha/beta) cores with charged/polar residues on solvent faces.
- 2‑oxoglutarate/Fe(II)‑dependent dioxygenases: peripheral helices and charged surface patches flanking the jelly‑roll core.
- Peptidases/metalloproteases and oligopeptidases (M3 family / mitochondrial intermediate peptidases): helical scaffold surfaces with peaks on charged residues; activation also includes the HExxH zinc-binding histidine region.
- Methylmalonyl‑CoA mutase system: inter‑subunit alpha‑helical surfaces and charged patches mediating assembly.
- Viral head/portal/tail structural proteins: long coiled‑coils and helical bundles with enrichment on exposed charged residues along the coiled‑coil surface.
- Myosin motor proteins: coiled‑coil tail and helical subdomains of the motor decorated with charged residues; signal tracks along long ordered helices.
- Glycine cleavage system P protein: external helices of the PLP enzyme scaffold.
- PLP‑dependent decarboxylases: solvent-exposed helices and multimer interface helices.

- DNA polymerases (cellular/archaeal/viral) and LigD: helical subdomains (thumb/fingers/auxiliary helices) and DNA/protein interface surfaces; peaks on K/R/E/D outside catalytic acidic motifs.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (GH31, GH3, alpha‑L‑fucosidase, 4‑alpha‑glucanotransferase): external helices around (alpha/beta) cores with charged/polar residues on solvent faces.
- 2‑oxoglutarate/Fe(II)‑dependent dioxygenases: peripheral helices and charged surface patches flanking the jelly‑roll core.
- Peptidases/metalloproteases and oligopeptidases (M3 family / mitochondrial intermediate peptidases): helical scaffold surfaces with peaks on charged residues; activation also includes the HExxH zinc-binding histidine region.
- Methylmalonyl‑CoA mutase system: inter‑subunit alpha‑helical surfaces and charged patches mediating assembly.
- Viral head/portal/tail structural proteins: long coiled‑coils and helical bundles with enrichment on exposed charged residues along the coiled‑coil surface.
- Myosin motor proteins: coiled‑coil tail and helical subdomains of the motor decorated with charged residues; signal tracks along long ordered helices.
- Glycine cleavage system P protein: external helices of the PLP enzyme scaffold.
- PLP‑dependent decarboxylases: solvent-exposed helices and multimer interface helices.

11667.label: Mid-protein functional core
11667.summary: Long, contiguous internal “core” modules enriched in hydrophobic/ aromatic residues: in multipass membrane proteins this corresponds to the main transmembrane bundle and adjacent gating/ligand‑binding loops; in soluble enzymes it aligns with the central catalytic/metal‑binding domain.
11667.description:
Summary: Long, contiguous internal “core” modules enriched in hydrophobic/ aromatic residues: in multipass membrane proteins this corresponds to the main transmembrane bundle and adjacent gating/ligand‑binding loops; in soluble enzymes it aligns with the central catalytic/metal‑binding domain.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across a single mid‑protein segment (typically ~100–200 aa), often spanning α‑helices (including TM helices) with spillover into adjacent loops; flanking N‑ and C‑terminal regions are weak. Peaks often occur on helical segments and nearby flexible loops, including membrane‑interface/kink positions (Gly/Trp/Pro), and encompass annotated functional sites (PTMs, glycosylation, disulfides, metal-binding).
Exemplars: - Gap junction/pannexin channels: strong activation on the large intracellular TM2–TM3 loop and TM3 gating helix.
- Bestrophin Ca2+-activated channels: activated cytosolic helical domain immediately preceding the final TM.
- P2X ligand-gated channels: activated extracellular ligand-binding ectodomain including disulfide/glycosylation sites and ATP-binding residues.
- Bacterial respiratory/redox multipass subunits (e.g., sulfite dehydrogenase C): activated central tri‑helix membrane bundle and connecting loops.
- Ceramide synthase/LAG1/TLC family: activation within the TLC domain covering a TM helix, the adjacent loop, and following helix that form the functional core.
- tRNA pseudouridine synthase D (TruD): activation across the TRUD fold constituting the catalytic/binding core.
- CRISPR Cas1 endonuclease: activated helical core containing the divalent metal-binding catalytic residues.

5938.label: Domain-boundary tethering segments
5938.summary: Boundary regions—often short helical elements or flexible linkers—that occur immediately adjacent to domains (often just C‑terminal to small zinc-binding modules or at the N-terminus of catalytic/DNA-binding cores such as SANT or the Nudix box) and serve as interaction/tethering segments across diverse proteins.
5938.description:
Summary: Boundary regions—often short helical elements or flexible linkers—that occur immediately adjacent to domains (often just C‑terminal to small zinc-binding modules or at the N-terminus of catalytic/DNA-binding cores such as SANT or the Nudix box) and serve as interaction/tethering segments across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous stretches. Signal is prominent at disorder-to-order transitions entering a domain and on short α-helices flanking metal-binding modules; it can also cover small helical DNA-binding modules (SANT). Activation typically avoids the compact metal-binding core itself and peaks just downstream of it or just upstream of conserved catalytic motifs.
Exemplars: - Transcription initiation factor TFIIE-alpha: activation on a long helix-to-coil segment immediately C-terminal to a C4 zinc finger, tapering into a disordered region.
- Transcription elongation factor SPT4: activation across the C-terminal half centered on a conserved W-V-A-R-W-containing region; no activation on the N-terminal C4 zinc finger.
- SWI/SNF subunit RSC8: strong activation spanning the SANT DNA-binding domain that follows a degenerate ZZ-type zinc finger; peak within an alpha-helix.
- GNAT N-acetyltransferase: activation at the disorder-to-order transition entering the N-terminus of the catalytic GNAT domain.
- Nudix hydrolase: activation across the region containing the conserved Nudix box and Mg2+-binding acidic residues, peaking just upstream of the motif.
- tRNA(Ile2) agmatinylcytidine synthetase (TiaS): activation on a low-confidence, flexible C-terminal tail.
- CRISPR type III Cas10/Csm1: activation on a long, highly disordered inter-domain linker between nuclease cores and the C-terminal GGDEF domain.
